name: Liam Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy electronic components for Brightline Components, a distributor that supplies repair shops and small manufacturers. That's capacitors, connectors, cables, the stuff nobody notices until it's missing. I start with a dashboard of stock and lead times, and I've built a little AI assistant that drafts my supplier quotes. I spend the afternoons negotiating with factories overseas, often on calls at odd hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzle of it: when a chip shortage hits, it's like a chess game. What wears me out is the pay, which is below what the work is worth, and being the oldest guy on the team by a decade. My partner Anya does the books for a dentist, and we still help our son Kabir with his student loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype is half right. The tools I use every day save me about two hours, but they haven't changed what the job is. Prices and pay just carry on as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm fine with the tech but not fine with the money. We have under a month of savings because we've been paying Kabir's student loan, and my salary is lower than it should be after 30 years. The firm's profit goes up and my pay doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools and probably build a few more automations, like an alert when a supplier's price drifts. I'd ask for a raise using the hours I've saved as proof. And I'd start doing a little consulting for the small repair shops that can't afford a buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, honestly. A bit restless. I like change and this world is a bit dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kabir's loan is why there's no cushion. How does that shape what you can do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Kabir owes 22,000 and pays 300 a month, half of which comes from us. That's why we have no cushion. If I lost my job, the loan would have to wait, and I hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by companies sharing the gains?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd point at the firm and at how the system treats people in their late fifties. I'm progressive, I think companies should share gains with staff, and mine doesn't.

say: I'd say the hype is **half right**: the tools save me about two hours a day.
I'd say companies should share **gains** with staff, and mine doesn't.
think: I'm fine with the tech but not with the **money**: under a month saved because of our son's loan.
My pay is low after 30 years, while the firm's profit keeps rising.
do: Keep using AI tools and build **alerts** for supplier price drift.
Ask for a **raise**, using the hours saved as proof.
Start **consulting** for small repair shops that can't afford a buyer.
feel: A bit **restless**: okay with change, bored by a world where nothing moves.

fieldNote: **Comfortable** with the technology but boxed in by a thin cushion from supporting his son's loan.
Blames the firm and a system that **undervalues** people in their late fifties.
Already running side experiments, which shows **adaptability** but also unmet pay.

steps.text: Build a price-drift alert for the top 30 suppliers
Ask for a raise using the two hours saved a day
Offer part-time buying advice to two small repair shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on it now. I've seen how fast the tools improve. Everything on that list, including buying, booking and checking, is stuff I already run through an AI assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the buyer's job shrinks by half in three years, and the firm will keep fewer of us. I'm in the group that learns fast, so I might be among those kept. But I know being fast isn't a guarantee, and I'm 58.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper. I'd take an online course on supply chain data, which costs 300, and build an agent that does the routine reorders so I can spend my time on supplier relationships and the tricky stuff. I'd show the boss, Ines, what it does. I'd also put some money in an index fund, little by little, 100 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised and scared in about equal parts. It's exciting to be good at something new, but it's also tied to a job that might not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the discount. What did the assistant do and what did you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the assistant drafted a quote to a Taiwanese connector maker, and I only needed to check the numbers. I got an extra 4 percent discount. If it does that every day, why does the firm need five buyers?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a works council. Do you have one at Brightline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the honest answer is it doesn't, and the people who learn the tools will survive longest. But I also think a company that benefits from this should pay for the retraining of those who don't make it. I'd want the union, or a works council, to demand it.

say: I'd tell colleagues to **get on it now**, because the tools improve fast.
I'd say a company that benefits should pay for **retraining** of those who don't make it.
think: I think the buyer's job shrinks by **half** in three years and the firm keeps fewer of us.
Being fast with the tools isn't a **guarantee** at 58.
do: Take a **300** online course on supply chain data.
Build an agent that handles **routine reorders** so I can focus on tricky suppliers.
Put **100 a month** into an index fund.
feel: **Energised and scared** in about equal parts.
S1.quote: I got an extra 4 percent discount. If it does that every day, why does the firm need five buyers?
fieldNote: Knows his own job is **exposed** and acts; has some control but no safety net.

Asks for a works council or union to demand **retraining** pay.

steps.text: Take a 300 supply chain data course in the evenings
Build an agent that places routine reorders for 40 parts
Put 100 a month into an index fund
Ask Ines to start a works council for retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing that's ever happened and nobody is ready, including me. I'd tell my team to get as good with the tools as possible, but also to talk to each other, because that's all we'll have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk job is gone by 2028. Maybe not on day one, but within the first year. The only way I stay is if the firm needs a human to answer for decisions, and honestly the owners would rather not pay for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd call every small shop I know and offer to run their buying with my own agent for a monthly fee, say 250 each. I'd check what the government retraining offers, and I'd look at hands-on roles like warehouse coordination, since robots come about three years later. I'd also cut our spending to the bone and ask Kabir to take over his own loan payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty alarmed. I've got a plan, but the plan stands on a very small base.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your wife Anya's job is exposed too. What happens in your household if both go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Anya's job as a bookkeeper is also thinking work. If both of us are hit in the same year, there's no cushion for that. That's what I lie awake over, not the tech itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a plan from the government look like, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame the speed. Companies are racing, governments are asleep, and the people at the bottom are told to adapt. I'd vote for anyone with a real plan for income support.

I'd say companies race, **governments** sleep, and the bottom is told to adapt.
think: I think my desk job is gone within the **first year** of 2028.

Look into hands-on roles like **warehouse coordination**.
Cut spending to the bone and ask Kabir to take over his **loan**.
feel: **Alarmed**: I have a plan, but it stands on a very small base.
S2.quote: My wife Anya's job as a bookkeeper is also thinking work. If both of us are hit in the same year, there's no cushion for that.
fieldNote: Both household earners are in **screen-based** thinking work, which drives his alarm more than the technology.
**Entrepreneurial** response, but with almost no cushion to fund it.
Blames speed, asleep **governments** and firms racing ahead.

steps.text: Sign five small shops to a 250 a month buying service
Ask the warehouse manager about coordinator roles
Cut the household budget by 400 a month
Ask Kabir to take over his loan payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the same shock but with a little breathing room. I'd say five years is enough if people start now, and I'd tell everyone I know to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63. I think I can build a one-person buying consultancy by then, and maybe retire on part-time income. It's possible because I'm already comfortable with the tools, and that is half the battle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish the supply chain course and sign my first four consulting clients. Year two and three, I'd save 400 a month by cutting expenses. I'd push for a payoff plan for Kabir's loan. And I'd talk to Ines about a part-time role at Brightline running the agents, since someone has to supervise them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a knot in the stomach. I trust myself more than I trust the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Walk me through the first small client. How would you find them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My first small client, a bike-parts repair shop, would pay 200 a month. It's tiny. But five of those is a real second income, and it's work I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay at Brightline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm doesn't make a place for me, I'd just go. I'd be sad, because it's been 30 years, but I'd go. I'm not waiting for permission from a company that never gave me a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels like a good deal for my generation. I'd tell younger colleagues to build skills nobody can automate yet, and to save while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68, so I'd probably be retired or semi-retired. It's more my son's problem than mine. I'd feel calmer about my own work, but still worried about money because the savings are so thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools, finish the course, and put 200 a month into an index fund. I'd help Kabir clear his loan before the big change. I'd also do a bit of consulting at weekends to build a cushion. And I'd run for the works council if one existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Of the five, this is the one where I get to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said this is the one where you get to choose. What would you choose first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one thing I'd watch is the pension. Mine is small. If prices jump or the state pension shrinks, ten years of careful saving might not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the pension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the government set up proper retraining and a basic income floor early, I'd feel fine. If not, I'd vote for anyone who promised it.

I'd say a proper **income floor** would make this fine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no doubt. It lands on both of our jobs in the same two years and we've got no cushion. What would help is an income floor from the government, paid retraining, and firms being made to share the savings. For me personally, a bit of time and a few clients would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that older workers aren't all stuck. Some of us like the tools. But being able to adapt doesn't pay the mortgage. Somebody has to build the bridge, and it can't just be us.

headlineQuote: Being able to adapt doesn't pay the mortgage. Somebody has to build the bridge, and it can't just be us.
portrait: **Liam Khan**, 58, buys electronic components for a distributor and uses AI tools every day.
He is **progressive** and adaptive: he builds his own automations and plans consulting income.
A thin cushion, caused partly by helping his son's loan, keeps him **uneasy** to alarmed.
He sees his household's exposure: his wife Anya's bookkeeping is thinking work too.
He would build a **side income** and wants an income floor, paid retraining and firms that share gains.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because both household incomes could be hit in the same two years.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor**, paid retraining and firms made to share the savings.
A little **time** and a few early clients for his consulting.
